screens.title: Developing Chaincode on Hyperledger Fabric
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn what chaincode is, why it matters for business logic on Hyperledger Fabric, and the core building blocks you will implement when writing chaincode in Go. Chaincode is the smart contract layer that enforces rules for assets and transactions; it runs inside isolated containers so every endorsing peer executes the same code. You will see the two required entry points every chaincode must provide — the initialization function used at deploy time and the invoke function used for normal transactions — and how they connect to ledger APIs like put state, get state, and delete state. We also walk through a compact Go example that implements a basic Asset model and common CRUD patterns. Finally, we preview the Fabric v2. x lifecycle: packaging the code, installing it on peers, collecting organization approvals, and committing the definition so clients can call your contract. By the end you will know how to structure chaincode, avoid non-deterministic pitfalls, and extend the example with a transfer function that updates asset ownership.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Developing Chaincode
Developing Chaincode on Hyperledger Fabric
Implement deterministic business logic with Init, Invoke, and ledger APIs.
In this lesson

You will inspect a Go chaincode example, learn ledger interactions with PutState/GetState/DelState, and follow the v2.x lifecycle commands to publish chaincode safely across organizations.

Why it matters

Chaincode defines the immutable rules for assets and determines whether transactions validate. Correct structure and deterministic code prevent validation failures and governance issues.

Explore Key Topics
Chaincode Structure
Init and Invoke form the contract surface for all transactions.
Ledger APIs
PutState, GetState, DelState manage JSON-marshaled key-value assets.
Lifecycle
Package, install, approve, and commit to make chaincode active.
Concept map: Execution model
Chaincode runs in isolated containers on endorsing peers; transactions are proposed, endorsed, ordered, and validated against an endorsement policy.
Input
Transaction proposal with function name and args.
Processing
Invoke routes to helper functions and uses stub APIs to read/write state.
Output
Transaction read/write sets returned for endorsement and ordering.
Safety
Avoid non-determinism such as timestamps or random numbers inside chaincode.
Key Takeaway

Chaincode is the deterministic rule-set for your application. Structure Init and Invoke carefully and use ledger APIs consistently to maintain integrity across peers.

screens.title: What is Chaincode?
screens.narratorSegment: Chaincode is the programmable business logic that runs on endorsing peers and shapes what transactions do to the ledger. Think of it as a deterministic function executed by multiple peers: given the same inputs and state, each peer must reach the same result. Chaincode is written in Go, Node. js, or Java and runs in an isolated container so execution remains consistent across peers. A concrete example is an asset contract that manages items using keys and JSON-marshaled values; every create, read, update, or delete goes through chaincode. A common misconception is that chaincode is the same as the ledger—it is not: the ledger stores state, while chaincode defines how that state changes. Another error is treating chaincode as a place for secrets or external calls; because peers must produce identical results, you should avoid randomness, timestamps, or direct external A P I calls. If external data is essential, use an off-chain oracle pattern. In practice, designing chaincode requires clear data models, careful validation of inputs, and explicit checks for existence before writes. Reflect: what parts of your business logic must be deterministic and auditable to belong inside chaincode?

keyIdea.text: Chaincode encapsulates deterministic business rules and runs on each endorsing peer to produce consistent read/write sets.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › What is Chaincode?
Core definition

Chaincode defines how transactions transform ledger state. It runs in containers on endorsing peers and must be deterministic so endorsements match.

Analogy

Treat chaincode as the business rule engine and the ledger as the database. The engine decides allowed changes; the database records them.

Common misconception

Don't place external secrets or non-deterministic calls inside chaincode; those break endorsement consensus.

Concrete example
An asset contract stores items by ID as JSON. Create checks GetState to ensure the ID doesn't exist, serializes the asset to JSON, then PutState to save it. Read uses GetState and returns the stored JSON bytes.
Key Takeaway

Chaincode must be deterministic, validate inputs, and use ledger APIs to keep world state consistent across peers.

screens.title: Init and Invoke: The Chaincode Interface
screens.narratorSegment: Every Fabric chaincode implements a Chaincode interface with two required functions: Init and Invoke. Init runs during instantiation or an upgrade. It's often used to write initial world state, record a version string, or perform setup tasks needed before normal transactions occur. For example, you might set an initial administrative account or seed a set of assets. A frequent mistake is to put time-sensitive logic or non-idempotent initialization in Init; remember instantiation may be repeated during upgrades and must not produce divergent state when called by different organizations. Invoke handles all subsequent transaction proposals. It inspects the requested function name and arguments, routes to helper methods like createAsset or readAsset, and returns shim. Success or shim. Error. Best practice is to validate argument counts immediately, return descriptive errors, and perform existence checks using GetState before PutState or DelState. A common pattern in Go is to use a switch on the function name and delegate work to methods that each return peer. Response. Reflect: when you design Invoke routing, how will you surface clear errors to clients and avoid unexpected overwrites?

keyIdea.title: Interface rules
keyIdea.text: Init sets up state at instantiation; Invoke routes transactions and must validate inputs and existence to protect world state.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Init & Invoke
Init — initialization

Called on instantiation or upgrade. Use it for seeding state or storing a version marker. Avoid non-deterministic operations here.

Check
  • Keep Init idempotent where possible.
  • Record version info to support upgrades.
  • Don't call external services directly.
Invoke — routing and helpers

Invoke receives a function name and arguments, routes to helpers, and returns a response. Validate args early and route with a clear switch or map to avoid ambiguous behavior.

// pseudo-Go invoke routing
function, args := stub.GetFunctionAndParameters()
switch function {
case "createAsset":
    return t.createAsset(stub, args)
case "readAsset":
    return t.readAsset(stub, args)
default:
    return shim.Error("Invalid chaincode function name")
}
Example practice

Implement argument count checks in each helper to return helpful errors when clients submit malformed requests.

Misconception

Don't assume Invoke will only be called in a single order; treat each invocation as independent and validate state each time.

screens.title: Ledger APIs: PutState, GetState, DelState
screens.narratorSegment: Interacting with the ledger inside chaincode uses the ChaincodeStubInterface methods GetState, PutState, and DelState. GetState(key) returns the byte value for a key or nil if not found; use it to check existence and to read stored JSON. PutState(key, value) writes or overwrites a key's value; always ensure you meant to overwrite by checking existence first when appropriate. DelState(key) removes a key from the world state; validate the key is present before deleting to avoid no-op surprises. In practice you often store JSON-marshaled structs: marshal your struct to bytes, then PutState. On read, GetState returns bytes you can unmarshal back into your struct. Error handling is essential: every call may return an error that should be wrapped into shim. Error with a descriptive message. A common mistake is assuming GetState returning nil is an error—nil means the key doesn't exist, which you should handle explicitly. Here's a short pseudo-flow: when creating an asset, call GetState to ensure non-existence; if nil, marshal and PutState; on update, GetState must return bytes, unmarshal, modify fields, marshal again, and PutState. What's one validation you will always add before writing state?

keyIdea.title: Ledger APIs
keyIdea.text: Use GetState to read and check keys, PutState to write JSON bytes, and DelState to remove keys; always handle returned errors.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Ledger APIs
Read, write, delete

GetState returns bytes or nil. PutState writes bytes for a key. DelState removes a key. Always check errors, and validate existence before destructive operations.

Common pattern
  • GetState key → if bytes == nil then create, else error.
  • On update: GetState, unmarshal, modify, marshal, PutState.
  • On delete: GetState ensures existence, then DelState.
Code example
// readAsset example (Go style)
assetAsBytes, err := stub.GetState(assetID)
if err != nil {
    return shim.Error(fmt.Sprintf("Failed to get asset: %s", err.Error()))
}
if assetAsBytes == nil {
    return shim.Error(fmt.Sprintf("Asset with ID %s does not exist", assetID))
}
return shim.Success(assetAsBytes)

// put example: marshal a struct then
err = stub.PutState(assetID, assetJSONasBytes)
if err != nil {
    return shim.Error(err.Error())
}
Key Takeaway

Treat GetState nil as "not found" and check before writes or deletes to avoid data integrity issues.

Pitfall

Not checking GetState before PutState can silently overwrite existing assets.

Pro tip

Wrap JSON marshal/unmarshal errors into shim.Error with context to help client debugging.

The readAsset helper expects a single argument, calls GetState, and returns an error if the asset is not present. Notice how the code uses descriptive shim. Error messages to aid clients in knowing what went wrong. A frequent mistake is to skip size or type conversions; in production convert and validate numeric strings explicitly. Also note the example temporarily hardcodes size; in a real contract you should parse and validate the size input. As you study the code, ask: how will you structure error messages so that clients can handle failures gracefully without leaking sensitive internal state? Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Adding transferAsset
Invoke routing change
// add to Invoke routing
} else if function == "transferAsset" {
    return t.transferAsset(stub, args)
}
Ensure the error message includes expected arguments and that the default error lists available functions.
transferAsset implementation
func (t *SimpleChaincode) transferAsset(stub shim.ChaincodeStubInterface, args []string) peer.Response {
    if len(args) != 2 {
        return shim.Error("Incorrect number of arguments. Expecting 2: Asset ID, New Owner")
    }
    assetID := args[0]
    newOwner := args[1]
    assetAsBytes, err := stub.GetState(assetID)
    if err != nil { return shim.Error(fmt.Sprintf("Failed to get asset: %s", err.Error())) }
    if assetAsBytes == nil { return shim.Error(fmt.Sprintf("Asset with ID %s does not exist", assetID)) }
    asset := Asset{}
    err = json.Unmarshal(assetAsBytes, &asset)
    if err != nil { return shim.Error(err.Error()) }
    asset.Owner = newOwner
    assetJSONasBytes, err := json.Marshal(asset)
    if err != nil { return shim.Error(err.Error()) }
    err = stub.PutState(assetID, assetJSONasBytes)
    if err != nil { return shim.Error(err.Error()) }
    return shim.Success(nil)
}
Scenario

Client calls transferAsset with ID "asset1" and owner "bob". The chaincode updates owner and persists the change using PutState.

Pitfall

If you skip GetState existence checks, transfer will fail silently or produce confusing errors when unmarshalling nil bytes.

Pro tip

Consider adding access control so only the current owner or an authorized role can transfer an asset.

screens.title: Chaincode Lifecycle (v2.x)
screens.narratorSegment: Fabric v2. x introduces a lifecycle that emphasizes governance: organizations must agree on chaincode definitions before it becomes active. The lifecycle steps are package, install, approvefororg, and commit. Packaging produces a tarball containing your chaincode sources and a label. Install places the package on each endorsing peer's filesystem and returns a package ID used for approval. Each organization then calls approveformyorg to record its endorsement of the chaincode definition, which includes name, version, sequence, and endorsement policy. Once a sufficient set of organizations have approved per the channel policy, one organization calls commit to make the definition active on the channel. A concrete command sequence shows packaging to mycc. tar. gz, installing to obtain a package ID, and then approving and committing. A common confusion is thinking install alone enables chaincode; until commit runs, client invocations will fail because the channel has no active definition. This lifecycle enforces multi-organization governance, so plan versioning and endorsement policies ahead of time to avoid deployment rollback friction. Chaincode Lifecycle (v2.x) means v2.x lifecycle requires packaging, peer installs, per-org approvals, and commit to activate chaincode on a channel.. In practical terms, package, install, approve, and commit to activate chaincode. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Chaincode Lifecycle
Lifecycle steps
  1. Package chaincode to a tarball and label it.
  2. Install the package on each endorsing peer to get package ID.
  3. Each org calls approveformyorg with package ID and definition details.
  4. One org calls commit after sufficient approvals to make it active.
Important

Install alone does not activate chaincode; commit is the final step that makes the definition callable by clients.

Command snippets
peer lifecycle chaincode package mycc.tar.gz --path ./chaincode --lang golang --label mycc_1.0
peer lifecycle chaincode install mycc.tar.gz
peer lifecycle chaincode approveformyorg -o orderer.example.com:7050 --channelID mychannel --name mycc --version 1.0 --package-id mycc_1.0:abcdef... --sequence 1 --tls --cafile $ORDERER_CA
peer lifecycle chaincode commit -o orderer.example.com:7050 --channelID mychannel --name mycc --version 1.0 --sequence 1 --tls --cafile $ORDERER_CA --peerAddresses peer0.org1.example.com:7051
Governance note

Plan endorsement policies and sequence numbers to coordinate upgrades across organizations smoothly.

Common mistake

Assuming install equals activation; until commit runs, invocations will be rejected by the channel configuration.

screens.title: Determinism, Security, and Error Handling
screens.narratorSegment: Two themes are critical when writing chaincode: deterministic execution and secure handling of sensitive data. Determinism means every endorsing peer must produce the same read/write set for a given transaction proposal. Avoid using random numbers, current timestamps, or direct external A P I calls inside chaincode, because they can diverge results across peers and cause transaction validation to fail. If you need off-chain data, adopt an oracle pattern where an off-chain signer records trusted data onto the ledger and chaincode consumes that recorded value. For security, never store private keys or credentials inside chaincode; use external secret stores and pass ephemeral references as needed. Error handling should be explicit: return shim. Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Determinism & Security
Determinism
  • Avoid using current time or random numbers inside chaincode.
  • Do not call external APIs directly from chaincode.
  • Use oracle or off-chain signing patterns for external data.
Security & errors
  • Never store private keys or credentials in chaincode.
  • Return shim.Error messages that are descriptive but do not leak secrets.
  • Validate all input conversions and handle marshal/unmarshal errors explicitly.
Check

If you must use external data, write it to the ledger via a trusted signer and then read it from chaincode, preserving determinism.

Mistake

Using time.Now or random numbers in chaincode leads to endorsement mismatches across peers and transaction failures.

Practice

Add unit tests for helper functions and simulate GetState/PutState interactions to catch marshal errors early.

screens.narratorSegment: This slide compares common mistakes with recommended practices. Mistake one is not checking GetState before PutState, which can overwrite existing data; the correct approach is to check existence and return an error when creating duplicates. Mistake two is poor error messages that reveal internals or omit actionable hints; instead return clear, non-sensitive messages that help a client choose a corrective action. Mistake three is placing secrets or external A P I calls inside chaincode; instead store references to secrets in a secure store or use an oracle pattern for external data. Mistake four is allowing any caller to perform sensitive actions; implement access control checks inside chaincode, for example verifying the transaction submitter's identity or roles before transferring an asset. screens.title: Designing Chaincode for Production
screens.narratorSegment: When moving chaincode into production, think beyond single transactions. Design a stable data model: pick clear keys, consistent JSON field names, and avoid changing types abruptly between versions. Record a version marker in Init so upgrades can detect and migrate older formats. For governance, define endorsement policies that reflect your organizational trust model and keep upgrade sequences coordinated to avoid split approvals. Use the lifecycle to coordinate installs and approvals across organizations and increase the sequence number only when you intentionally change the definition. Plan for migrations by writing upgrade helpers that transform stored JSON safely and use deterministic logic during migration. For monitoring and debugging, add structured logs in development but avoid leaking secrets. Finally, perform security reviews to ensure no sensitive data is stored on-chain and that access control is enforced at the contract level. Ask yourself: does this contract need strict endorsement, or can looser policies speed up operations without weakening trust? In this lesson you will learn what chaincode is, why it matters for business logic on Hyperledger Fabric, and the core building blocks you will implement when writing chaincode in Go. Chaincode is the smart contract layer that enforces rules for assets and transactions; it runs inside isolated containers so every endorsing peer executes the same code. You will see the two required entry points every chaincode must provide — the initialization function used at deploy time and the invoke function used for normal transactions — and how they connect to ledger APIs like put state, get state, and delete state. We also walk through a compact Go example that implements a basic Asset model and common CRUD patterns. Finally, we preview the Fabric v2. x lifecycle: packaging the code, installing it on peers, collecting organization approvals, and committing the definition so clients can call your contract. By the end you will know how to structure chaincode, avoid non-deterministic pitfalls, and extend the example with a transfer function that updates asset ownership.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain the role of chaincode in Hyperledger Fabric, implement the two required entry points in Go, and use the Fabric ledger APIs to manage state safely. You will write and read key-value JSON objects using PutState and GetState, handle deletion with DelState, and design checks that prevent accidental overwrites. You will also understand the Fabric v2. x lifecycle so you can package, install, collect approvals, and commit chaincode definitions across organizations. Each objective focuses on a practical skill: structuring chaincode, implementing CRUD patterns with correct error handling, applying lifecycle commands to publish your contract, and recognizing non-determinism or security risks. These skills let you build production-ready contracts that validate consistently across peers and fit governance rules. You'll finish with a hands-on task to add and test a transfer function that changes asset ownership, reinforcing both code and lifecycle skills.

These objectives break down into concrete skills you can practice and test. First, you'll write an Init function to set initial state or version data during instantiation. That matters because initial ledger shape often determines later validation. Second, you'll implement Invoke routing to helper functions and validate argument counts to avoid malformed calls. Third, you'll use GetState to check existence before writes and DelState to remove keys safely, which prevents accidental overwrites and maintains integrity. Fourth, you'll follow the Fabric v2. x lifecycle: packaging, installing on peers, approving definitions per organization, and committing the definition. Each of these is practical: the Init and Invoke code runs on every endorsing peer, the ledger APIs determine what the world state holds, and the lifecycle ensures multi-org governance. We'll measure success with code-level checks and a hands-on transfer function task so you can run through the full cycle conceptually and spot common mistakes.

Chaincode is the programmable business logic that runs on endorsing peers and shapes what transactions do to the ledger. Think of it as a deterministic function executed by multiple peers: given the same inputs and state, each peer must reach the same result. Chaincode is written in Go, Node. js, or Java and runs in an isolated container so execution remains consistent across peers. A concrete example is an asset contract that manages items using keys and JSON-marshaled values; every create, read, update, or delete goes through chaincode. A common misconception is that chaincode is the same as the ledger—it is not: the ledger stores state, while chaincode defines how that state changes. Another error is treating chaincode as a place for secrets or external calls; because peers must produce identical results, you should avoid randomness, timestamps, or direct external A P I calls. If external data is essential, use an off-chain oracle pattern. In practice, designing chaincode requires clear data models, careful validation of inputs, and explicit checks for existence before writes. Reflect: what parts of your business logic must be deterministic and auditable to belong inside chaincode?

Every Fabric chaincode implements a Chaincode interface with two required functions: Init and Invoke. Init runs during instantiation or an upgrade. It's often used to write initial world state, record a version string, or perform setup tasks needed before normal transactions occur. For example, you might set an initial administrative account or seed a set of assets. A frequent mistake is to put time-sensitive logic or non-idempotent initialization in Init; remember instantiation may be repeated during upgrades and must not produce divergent state when called by different organizations. Invoke handles all subsequent transaction proposals. It inspects the requested function name and arguments, routes to helper methods like createAsset or readAsset, and returns shim. Success or shim. Error. Best practice is to validate argument counts immediately, return descriptive errors, and perform existence checks using GetState before PutState or DelState. A common pattern in Go is to use a switch on the function name and delegate work to methods that each return peer. Response. Reflect: when you design Invoke routing, how will you surface clear errors to clients and avoid unexpected overwrites?

Interacting with the ledger inside chaincode uses the ChaincodeStubInterface methods GetState, PutState, and DelState. GetState(key) returns the byte value for a key or nil if not found; use it to check existence and to read stored JSON. PutState(key, value) writes or overwrites a key's value; always ensure you meant to overwrite by checking existence first when appropriate. DelState(key) removes a key from the world state; validate the key is present before deleting to avoid no-op surprises. In practice you often store JSON-marshaled structs: marshal your struct to bytes, then PutState. On read, GetState returns bytes you can unmarshal back into your struct. Error handling is essential: every call may return an error that should be wrapped into shim. Error with a descriptive message. A common mistake is assuming GetState returning nil is an error—nil means the key doesn't exist, which you should handle explicitly. Here's a short pseudo-flow: when creating an asset, call GetState to ensure non-existence; if nil, marshal and PutState; on update, GetState must return bytes, unmarshal, modify fields, marshal again, and PutState.
